reviewer: R1_editor (Handling Editor, Analytica Chimica Acta - desk assessment, cycle 02)
summary: This revision is clearly stronger than cycle 01. The paper now has a conceptual core: Proposition 1, an observability horizon below which analyte signal and noise cannot be told apart, so the gain from more samples is not identifiable from a pilot. A computable identification set and an information fraction operationalise it. B-RPM is a Bayesian forecaster with a structural prior on alignment and noise. The evidence is broad (38 public tasks), leakage-controlled and candid. No ACA paper in 2025-2026 addresses learning-curve forecasting or random-matrix theory, so the topic is unoccupied and in scope (calibration-set size, validation, reference-error floors). As submitted, however, the package has three desk-level problems. (1) The named method still loses to the trivial pilot-CV-error rule on accuracy. Three of four pre-specified hypotheses failed. Under the cross-family prior, B-RPM-LOFO is significantly worse than FLAT. The abstract, highlights and cover letter foreground 'least biased' and 'generalised' without saying so. (2) The headline transfer result changes only the soil tasks: LOFO is identical to LOSO for every non-soil family. It is significant only at task level (source level p = 0.64), and the abstract attaches the p-value to the wrong comparison. (3) The package would be returned before review for technical reasons: a duplicated cover letter with placeholders, author, CRediT, AI and funding placeholders, internal 'topic-selection record' and novelty-map material in the SI, references to non-existent tables, 'after the first review cycle' wording, and figure files whose names do not match their numbers. Proposition 1 is mathematically modest (a DE analogue of known noise-variance non-identifiability) but conceptually new and useful for analytical chemists. I judge the contribution to be at the ACA threshold, not clearly above it. With technical cleanup and honest recalibration of the claims, I would send it to review. In the current form the desk-reject risk is substantial.
strengths: Conceptual contribution new to chemometrics: an explicit observability horizon and a non-identifiability statement explain why power-law extrapolation is optimistic and why the no-improvement rule is hard to beat. The negative result is turned into a predicted one, as cycle 01 recommended.
The identification set and information fraction are computable per pilot, and the information fraction stratifies B-RPM error (0.373, 0.297, 0.188 by tertile), which gives a practical warning signal.
B-RPM is the only forecaster that stays nearly unbiased up to eightfold extrapolation (Fig. 7). IPL3 and the transferred slope grow increasingly optimistic and FLAT increasingly pessimistic.

Evidence base and rigour exceed most recent ACA method papers: 38 tasks from 8 provenance sources, group-disjoint splits, replicate averaging, repeated outer splits for small sets, a simulation with Monte-Carlo truth, task- and source-level statistics with Holm correction, and failed hypotheses reported.
The topic is unoccupied in ACA 2025-2026 and connects to live editorial themes (validation and leakage, reference-error floors, calibration-set size, unlabelled spectra).
A graphical abstract now exists. All eight figures are cited in order. Structured abstract format is followed.

issues.title: The named method still does not beat the trivial no-improvement rule on accuracy, and 3 of 4 pre-specified B-RPM hypotheses failed. The abstract, highlights and cover letter present it as the winning forecaster.
issues.description: The previous cycle's main desk-rejection risk is still there, only better hidden. On the primary level endpoint B-RPM (0.282) is worse than FLAT (0.262). HB2 non-inferiority (margin 0.02) failed. HB1 (gain, LOFO vs transferred slope) failed. HB3 (band coverage) failed. Only HB4 passed, and only on the pooled average. Under the strict cross-family prior that the paper calls its key generalisation result, B-RPM-LOFO is significantly worse than FLAT at both task and source level. On the gain endpoint, the transferred slope beats B-RPM in every family. On the decision endpoint no method beats the climatological base rate. The abstract, highlights and cover letter lead with 'least biased', 'kept its accuracy' and 'generalised', which are true only for the bias metric. A handling editor who opens Table 2 or Table S7 sees a named Bayesian method that loses to 'report the pilot CV error'. Under ACA's 'clear, quantifiable advantage' criterion, that is a desk-reject trigger.
issues.evidence: Table 2: level B-RPM 0.282 vs FLAT 0.262; gain B-RPM 0.265 vs SLOPE-T 0.188. Table S7: level B-RPM vs FLAT -0.020 (16/38 tasks, source 2/8). B-RPM-LOFO vs FLAT -0.030, Holm p=0.008, source p=0.023, 1/8 sources. Gain B-RPM vs SLOPE-T -0.077, 3/38 tasks, 0/8 sources. Table S8: FLAT has lower level error than B-RPM in fruit (0.168 vs 0.219), meat, mixture, pharma and soil; SLOPE-T has lower gain error in all six families. Section 4.6: Brier B-RPM 0.290 vs climatology 0.247. Sections 4.4-4.6: HB1, HB2 and HB3 not met.
issues.corrective_action: Make the knowledge contribution the headline: the observability horizon, the non-identifiability of the gain and the identification set. Present B-RPM as the forecaster that makes the unavoidable prior explicit and unbiased, not as the most accurate one. State in the abstract and highlights that the pilot's own CV error remains the most accurate level forecast, that B-RPM is not non-inferior to it, and that B-RPM's advantage is bias. Name the property that B-RPM uniquely delivers (unbiasedness across horizons, plus an information fraction that flags unreliable pilots) and quantify it as the advantage. Better still, add the decision analysis in issue 03 so that the advantage is decision-relevant.

issues.title: The cross-family transfer claim rests on soil tasks only, and its p-value is task-level, pseudo-replicated and attached to the wrong comparison in the abstract
issues.description: For every non-soil task, the LOFO prior or slope is identical to the LOSO one, because each non-soil family has only one source. Fig. 8 shows flat lines for all non-soil tasks in both panels, and Table S8 has identical LOSO/LOFO columns for fruit, fuel, meat, mixture and pharma. The 'strictest transfer test' therefore changes only the 23 soil tasks, which come from about 4 correlated sources, and asks one question: does a soil calibration tolerate a non-soil prior? The headline 'p = 0.001' compares B-RPM-LOFO with SLOPE-T-LOFO at task level (unadjusted; Holm p = 0.011). At the level of the eight sources, which the paper itself declares as the robustness check, it is +0.031, p = 0.641, 4/8 sources. The abstract also places 'p = 0.001' next to 'degraded to 0.392', which implies that the p-value tests the degradation. It does not. Highlight 5 and the cover letter generalise this to 'transferred across application families'.
issues.evidence: Fig. 8 (file Fig7_cross_family_transfer.png): non-soil lines are horizontal in both panels. Table S8: SLOPE-T and SLOPE-T-LOFO are identical in all non-soil families, as are B-RPM and B-RPM-LOFO. Table S7, row level B-RPM-LOFO vs SLOPE-T-LOFO: task p 0.001, Holm 0.011, source +0.031, p 0.641, 4/8. Abstract lines 23-24.
issues.corrective_action: State explicitly that LOFO differs from LOSO only for soil tasks. Report the soil-only comparison as the transfer result, with both task-level and source-level statistics, and give the Holm-adjusted value. Rewrite the abstract sentence so that the p-value is attached to the correct comparison. Reword Highlight 5, for example: 'A structural prior from non-soil calibrations kept B-RPM's accuracy on soil tasks; a transferred slope lost 0.18 log units'. Better still, make the test genuinely cross-family by adding non-soil families with more than one source (see proposed experiment).
issues.proposed_experiment: Add at least two independent public sources for each of two or three non-soil families, for example fruit/agri-food NIR (other public mango, apple and grain sets) and pharmaceutical tablets (other shoot-outs). Many are in the public collection behind Reiter et al. (ACA 2026, 66 NIR datasets). Then LOSO and LOFO differ for non-soil tasks as well, and the transfer test is no longer soil-only. Rerun B-RPM, B-RPM-LOFO, SLOPE-T and SLOPE-T-LOFO only; the existing pipeline is automated and each forecast takes about 0.2 s.

issues.title: The planning tool's practical value is asserted but never demonstrated on a decision endpoint
issues.description: The Significance statement and Conclusions recommend a staged design: a pilot of at least 100 samples, then a second batch when the identification set is wider than the decision requires. This rule is the paper's actionable output, but it is never evaluated. The only decision endpoint (Brier score of 'eightfold larger set reduces RMSEP by at least 15%') shows that no method beats the base rate. An identification set that covers about 90% while spanning a factor of 15 at eightfold extrapolation and 58 at 32-fold or more is close to uninformative unless it is shown to separate decidable from undecidable pilots. The information-fraction tertile analysis (0.373, 0.297, 0.188) is the only evidence of that, and it is one table in the SI.
issues.evidence: Section 4.3: width 3.4, 15 and 58. Section 4.6: Brier B-RPM 0.290 vs climatology 0.247. Section 4.3: tertile analysis, Table S12. Recommendations (ii)-(iii) and Conclusions are not evaluated.
issues.corrective_action: Evaluate the recommended staged rule retrospectively on the existing pilots and ground-truth curves. Report expected reference-sample cost and the rate of wrong go/no-go decisions against fixed rules (n=100, FLAT-based stop, SLOPE-T-based extension, IPL3) and against an oracle. Also report a selective-prediction curve: decision accuracy restricted to pilots whose identification set (or information fraction) passes the threshold, against the share of pilots retained. This turns the identification set into a measurable advantage.
issues.proposed_experiment: Computational only, using existing outputs. For each pilot, apply the rule 'if the identification-set width at the target n is below a threshold W (or the information fraction is above a threshold F), decide from B-RPM; otherwise draw a second batch of n0 and re-forecast'. Simulate the second batch by drawing additional pool samples. Compare decision regret, number of reference analyses and wrong-decision rate with FLAT, SLOPE-T, IPL3 and fixed-n rules, by family and at source level.

issues.title: Proposition 1 is mathematically elementary and closely parallels known non-identifiability of noise variance. The novelty is in the framing and must be stated precisely.
issues.description: The proof is a two-line inequality on the bias function within the deterministic-equivalent approximation. It is not a finite-sample statement, and the 'to first order in lambda_k/kappa_0' caveat sits outside the statement. Section 2.4 itself calls it a 'deterministic-equivalent analogue' of the noise-variance limits of Dicker and Janson et al. A theory-literate referee (ACA's chemometrics referees include statisticians such as Forzani, a co-author of a recent ACA paper) will ask what is new beyond (i) the DE risk (Dobriban & Wager; Hastie et al.), (ii) noise-variance non-identifiability (Dicker; EigenPrism) and (iii) Wei et al.'s use of empirical eigen-spectra. Combined, these ingredients are novel in chemometrics, and the observability horizon is a useful, citable concept. But the paper currently calls it a 'proof' and the cover letter calls it a 'methodological contribution' without saying how strong it is.
issues.evidence: Section 2.4, Proposition 1 and proof (lines 151-164). Text: 'Proposition 1 is a deterministic-equivalent analogue of the known limits of noise-variance estimation' (lines 179-181). Cover letter, contribution (i).
issues.corrective_action: Add a short 'what is new' paragraph with three bullets: new relative to DE risk theory, new relative to Dicker/EigenPrism, and new relative to Wei et al. Put the first-order/DE caveat inside the statement of the proposition. Give the horizon in a directly usable chemometric form: the n0-dependent eigenvalue cut-off, or equivalently the number of resolvable principal components, alongside the familiar PLS rank. Show on one real task that power hidden below the horizon is invisible in the pilot but appears at large n. This makes the result a chemometric insight, not a restatement of RMT.

issues.title: Abstract, highlights and cover letter overstate several numbers or omit the unfavourable half
issues.description: Specific mismatches. (a) 'Least biased forecaster (mean bias +0.008)': the overall mean nets out pessimism at short horizons against optimism at long ones (-0.134 at 32-fold or more is in the text, not the abstract), and the LOFO variant (+0.001) is less biased than the LOSO headline. (b) 'Identification set contained the true curve in ~9 of 10 cases': 91% is a task average just above the pre-specified 90% (HB4), coverage is 88% at 2x and 4x, and a set spanning a factor of 15 to 58 makes high coverage easy. The width must be reported beside the coverage in the highlights. (c) The cover letter says 'the first forecaster to use a transferable structural prior together with the task's unlabelled spectra'. A priority claim is unnecessary and invites challenge (LC-PFN priors, meta-learned curves by Turan et al. 2025). (d) The cover letter says 'all data and code are public, with a one-command rerun' and Section 2.5 says B-RPM was 'committed to the public repository', but the Data availability statement says code 'will be deposited in a public repository upon acceptance'. (e) 'Pre-registered' refers to an internal time-stamped file, not a registry; the previous cycle flagged this.
issues.evidence: Abstract lines 22-24 vs Section 4.4 (lines 434-436) and Table 2 (B-RPM-LOFO bias 0.001). Highlights 3 and 5. Fig. 6a. Cover letter paragraphs 3-4. Section 2.5 (lines 208-210) vs Data availability (lines 572-574).
issues.corrective_action: Add the long-horizon bias (-0.134 at 32-fold or more) and the FLAT comparison to the abstract. Pair coverage with width in Highlight 3 ('...but spanned a 15-fold RMSEP range at 8x'). Delete the 'first' claim. Either deposit code and data now with a DOI (Zenodo) and cite it, or remove every 'public repository' and 'all code public' statement. Replace 'pre-registered' with 'pre-specified in a time-stamped log (Supplementary Note 1)', unless a registry DOI exists.

issues.title: B-RPM performs worst where ACA's core readership works (pharma, mixtures, fuel), and the evidence base is 60% soil
issues.description: Per-family level errors for B-RPM are 0.387 (pharma), 0.569 (mixtures) and 0.350 (fuel), against 0.214 for soil. FLAT is better in pharma and mixtures, and IPL3 is better in mixtures. In Fig. 8b the non-soil tasks have B-RPM errors of 0.5-0.63. Band coverage after recalibration is 26% for mixtures. The paper discloses this in the limitations but generalises in the abstract to 'spectroscopy'. An ACA editor will note that the method is tuned on, and works for, large soil libraries, while the analytical-chemistry applications have small n and show the weakest results.
issues.evidence: Table S8 (level: pharma 0.387 vs FLAT 0.356; mixture 0.569 vs FLAT 0.474 and IPL3 0.360). Fig. 8b. Section 4.6: mixtures coverage 11% raw, 26% recalibrated. Limitation 5.
issues.corrective_action: Report per-family results in the main text (a compact version of Table S8). Narrow the abstract scope or state the soil dominance explicitly. Discuss why designed mixtures and small fuel sets violate the random-sampling premise, and say what an analyst with a designed calibration should do instead. Adding non-soil sources (issue 02) addresses this directly.

issues.title: Theory fit is weakest exactly in the pilot regime; the kappa-collapse figure contradicts the summary statistic
issues.description: Fig. 2a shows the DE curve systematically below the empirical ridge and PLS curves at n = 25-100 (about 20-25% low for KSSL-MIR:OC and Neospectra-NIR:pH), which is where pilots live. The mean absolute log error of 0.130 (about 14%) is larger than the typical gain per doubling (9.3%) that the planner wants to forecast. Fig. 2b shows a clear failure of the collapse at small kappa for n = 25-100 (curves fan out by up to an order of magnitude), yet the text reports an across-n SD of 0.037. The kappa range over which the SD is computed is not stated.
issues.evidence: Fig. 2a, four panels. Fig. 2b, small-kappa region. Section 4.1 (lines 333-345). Section 4.2: median slope -0.097 per doubling.
issues.corrective_action: State the kappa window used for the collapse SD and report the SD in the pilot-relevant window as well. Report the theory error stratified by n (25-100 vs 400 or more). Explain the small-n offset: the intercept, the df2/n approaching 1 regime and finite-n corrections. Discuss whether it propagates into the pilot path likelihood.

issues.title: Submission package would trigger an immediate technical return (placeholders, duplicated cover letter, internal workflow material in the SI)
issues.description: (a) The cover letter contains two salutations, two opening paragraphs with different article-type wording ('Research Paper' and 'research article'), two sign-offs, and unfilled [name]/[Department]/[Date] placeholders. (b) The manuscript has author, affiliation and corresponding-author placeholders, a CRediT block marked '(Placeholders - to be completed by the authors.)', an AI declaration with '(Authors: confirm or amend this statement...)', and 'Funding: [to be completed]'. (c) Supplementary Note 4 ('Literature matrix and novelty map', including a 'Topic-selection record' listing at least 15 screened candidate research directions and the internal file path manuscript/refs/verified_refs.json) is internal project material. It must not be submitted, and to an editor it reads as an AI-generated topic search. (d) Supplementary Note 3 cites 'Table S0' and 'sensitivity analysis S0', which do not exist. Internal experiment codes (E0-E7, 'version-2', 'first review cycle') appear in the main text and SI. (e) Section 3.6 mentions 'After the first review cycle', which exposes an earlier review history and is inappropriate in a first submission to ACA.
issues.evidence: cover_letter.pdf (duplicated blocks). manuscript_v3.txt lines 15-23, 561-564 and the AI/Funding statements. supplementary_full.md lines 1125-1200 (Notes 3-4). Section 3.6 line 290-291 ('After the first review cycle'), Sections 3.4/4.4 ('version-2 design').
issues.corrective_action: Rebuild the cover letter as a single, tailored letter. Fill in all author fields and declarations. Delete Supplementary Note 4 entirely. Fix the Table S0 references. Replace 'version 1/version 2', 'first review cycle' and E-codes with neutral design descriptions ('initial design', 'final design'). Describe AI use in the research process (code development, literature screening) in Methods as well, as Elsevier policy requires, not only in the writing declaration.

issues.title: Length, method proliferation and a 43-table SI dilute the message for an analytical readership
issues.description: The PDF is 36 pages, about 10,300 words including references. There are 17-19 forecaster variants (B-RPM, B-RPM-LOFO, -r, -0, -m10, RPM, RPM-w, RPM-T, RPM-TD, RPM-TP, IPL3, IPL2, EXP3, LOG2, WEI, FLAT, DF-OLS, SLOPE-T, SLOPE-T-LOFO). The SI has 43 tables, several of them about the superseded RPM design (S14-S31, S36-S43). Readers must track two study versions plus a post-hoc stage. The previous cycle already raised this (R9-C01-12), and it has grown rather than shrunk.
issues.evidence: Section 3.5 forecaster list; Table 2 (13 rows); supplementary_full.md Tables S1-S43; Section 3.6 three-stage design history.
issues.corrective_action: Aim for about 7,000 words of main text. Keep five forecasters in the main text (B-RPM, FLAT, SLOPE-T, IPL3, WEI) with B-RPM-LOFO as the transfer row. Move the RPM variants and ablations to one SI table. Archive the first-design analyses in a single 'initial design' SI section, or the repository, rather than 20 tables. Remove Section 3.6's narrative history and keep a two-sentence disclosure.

issues.title: Inconsistent counts and broken internal cross-references
issues.description: The Introduction says 'six public sources'. Section 3.7 and Table S7 use 'eight data sources'. Table 1 lists 11 libraries, and the internal analysis says 11 sources. Section 4.7 cites 'Section 2.4' for the ablation finding (that section is the observability horizon). Section 2.3 says RPM-w is introduced in 'Section 3.6', which does not define it. Some SI table citations point to legacy content: S32 is the first-design ablation, cited as current evidence.
issues.corrective_action: Define 'source' once (provenance; KSSL and NeoSpectra merged), give the number consistently (8), and fix all section and table cross-references.

issues.title: Figure file names do not match manuscript numbering; illustrative figures and the graphical abstract do not support the claims
issues.description: The figures directory holds Fig12_alignment_exponents (Fig. 3 in the text), Fig13_slope_vs_noise (Fig. 4), Fig3_identification_set_examples (Fig. 5), Fig5_observability (Fig. 6), Fig6_bias_by_horizon (Fig. 7) and Fig7_cross_family_transfer (Fig. 8), next to obsolete files with the same numbers (Fig3_example_forecasts, Fig4_main_accuracy, Fig5_error_vs_extrapolation_ratio, ...). Uploading these to Editorial Manager would almost certainly produce mismatched figures. In Fig. 5 (Mango:DM), B-RPM forecasts a 35% RMSEP reduction that does not occur and is visibly worse than the no-improvement rule. In the graphical abstract, B-RPM starts below the true curve at n0, is consistently optimistic, and power-law extrapolation is pessimistic, which contradicts the paper's message that IPL is optimistic. The GA is about 1330 x 500 px, below ACA's minimum of 531 x 1328 px (h x w).
issues.evidence: figures/ directory listing; Fig3_identification_set_examples.png middle panel; manuscript/Graphical_Abstract.png.
issues.corrective_action: Rename the figure files Fig1-Fig8 to match the text and delete obsolete files from the upload set. Choose a representative example for Fig. 5, or say explicitly that Mango shows a failure case. Redraw the GA as a schematic (horizon, identification set, prior), or use the median-error example where B-RPM is unbiased, at a size of at least 531 x 1328 px.

issues.title: Title is long and leads with the question rather than the deliverable
issues.description: The 27-word title combines three ideas. ACA editors scan titles for a method or tool.
issues.corrective_action: For example: 'Observability limits of calibration learning curves and Bayesian regularisation-path matching for sample-size planning in NIR/MIR spectroscopy'.

desk_decision: Borderline. As submitted: technical return to authors (package not compliant). After cleanup: send to review only if claims are recalibrated as in issues 01, 02 and 05.
recommendation: Do not submit in the current state. Fix the technical defects, recalibrate the framing around the observability result, and add the staged-decision evaluation before submitting. With those changes the estimated desk-reject probability falls to about 0.25-0.30.
recommendation_rationale: ACA desk decisions turn on (i) a fundamental methodological development with (ii) a quantifiable advantage over existing approaches. Point (i) is now plausibly met: the observability horizon and identification set are a genuine, unoccupied chemometric concept, even if the mathematics is a modest DE analogue of known results. Point (ii) is the weak link. On every accuracy endpoint, the named method is matched or beaten by reporting the pilot's CV error (level) or a transferred slope (gain). Its distinctive advantage, unbiasedness and cross-family robustness, is shown on bias only, and the robustness holds only for soil tasks at task level. An editor who reads the abstract and then Table 2 or Table S7 will feel oversold, and that, more than the negative result itself, drives desk rejection. Independently, the placeholders, the duplicated cover letter and the internal topic-selection record in the SI would cause a technical return and colour the editor's judgement. The six most effective changes are: (1) clean the package (issue 08) and rename the figure files; (2) rewrite the abstract, highlights and cover letter so that the observability limit is the headline, B-RPM's advantage is stated as bias, and FLAT superiority on level accuracy and soil-only transfer are disclosed with source-level statistics (issues 01, 02, 05); (3) evaluate the recommended staged design (identification-set or information-fraction threshold leading to a second batch) as decision regret and cost against FLAT, SLOPE-T, IPL3 and fixed-n rules (issue 03); this computational analysis on existing outputs is the most likely route to a quantifiable advantage; (4) add multi-source non-soil families so that cross-family transfer is tested beyond soil (issues 02 and 06); (5) shorten to about 7,000 words with five main forecasters, and cut the SI from 43 tables (issue 09); (6) add a precise 'what is new relative to DE theory, Dicker/EigenPrism and Wei et al.' paragraph, and state the horizon in chemometric terms (issue 04). If changes (2)-(3) cannot produce a decision-level advantage, CILS or J. Chemometrics is the safer venue.
